newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US seeks support to target China's rights record.
newsitem.headline: US seeks support to target China's rights record.

text.p: The United States and Denmark on Thursday pressed other member states of the U.N. Human Rights Commission to back their joint resolution criticising China's record and calling for reforms, officials from both states said.

But diplomatic sources said that support for the Western motion appeared to be eroding, making it increasingly likely that Beijing escapes censure again for the seventh straight year when the 53-member forum votes next Tuesday.
China was applying diplomatic pressure -- with commercial overtones -- to win backing for its own "no-action motion" which would pre-empt any vote on Denmark's text, they added.
China warned the United States on Thursday that relations could suffer if it continued to support Denmark's resolution at the U.N. body, which is holding its annual meeting in Geneva.
Denmark was due to formally present its draft text late in the day, co-sponsored by the United States and roughly 12 other countries, mainly European states, according to diplomats.
"It is a pretty tough game right now for votes..." Tyge Lehmann, head of Denmark's delegation to the 53-member forum, told Reuters shortly before he was due to deliver the motion.
"Some governments may not be willing to sponsor the text, but they might be more helpful in defending the resolution."
Lehmann, whose country has been praised by many diplomats for stepping forward to sponsor the resolution after the European Union backed away due to internal discord, added:
"We are really doing our best to defeat the Chinese no-action motion. We know China has been equally active."

An American official in Geneva told Reuters: "U.S. officials are optimistic on not losing the no-action motion. We are working energetically to get as many co-sponsors as possible for the Danish resolution.
"We are putting a full-court press on China," the American official added, using a basketball term. "The leaders of the State Department are commited to making this work."

The Danish draft resolution, obtained by Reuters, expresses concern at "continuing reports of violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms in China by local, provincial and national authorities and severe restrictions on the rights of citizens to the freedoms of assembly, association, expression and religion as well as to due legal process and to a fair trial."
It calls on Beijing to release political prisoners and protect the cultural and ethnic identity of Tibetans and others.
The text also calls on China to ratify two major international human rights treaties guaranteeing civil and political freedoms as well as economic and social rights.
A U.S. spokesman told Reuters that if Beijing wanted to improve its bilateral ties, a "good starting point" would be for it to make progress on improving respect for human rights.

"The U.S. is supporting Denmark's resolution because we believe that the Human Rights Commission is a fundamentally appropriate forum in which to discuss the human rights situation in China," a spokesman for the U.S. delegation in Geneva said.

"China knows this and it also knows that if it wants to improve bilateral relations with the United States, a good starting point would be for it to make progress on improving human rights in China," he added.

Australia announced on Thursday it had struck a deal with China to set up a formal bilateral dialogue on human rights, but revealed it would no longer back the Danish motion. Canada may also be edging away from supporting the text, diplomats said.
Both the United States and China have moved in recent months to ease strains over disputes ranging from Taiwan to trade and human rights that sent ties plummeting in 1995 and early 1996.

"Sino-U.S. relations have already seen improvements, but the U.S. support of Denmark will, of course, damage bilateral relations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.
"The U.S. government should resolve this problem from the basis of bilateral relations...Denmark should consider its national interests and consider seriously the consequences."

Both the Danish and Dutch Foreign Ministers were personally phoning their counterparts in key states which could swing the outcome of Tuesday's showdown, according to diplomatic sources. The Netherlands currently holds the EU presidency.
"We are still a few votes short of defeating a no-action motion," one European diplomat told Reuters. "We are lobbying in capitals at the level of Foreign Minister if not higher."
